title: The Great Hanoi Rat Hunt

lines.text: Hanoi once paid for rat tails. People started farming rats.
It was 1902, and French colonial Hanoi had new sewers full of breeding rats.
Plague was moving through the region, and rats carried the fleas that spread it.
So the authorities paid a small bounty for each rat. A severed tail counted as proof.
Before long, people noticed rats running about with no tails.
Hunters were cutting off the tails and letting the rats go, so they would breed more rats and more bounties.
Investigators later found rat farms in villages outside the city.
The bounty was abandoned. The rats stayed.
This is Goodhart's law. When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
A tail was a decent sign of a dead rat, right up until people were paid per tail.
Reward a number and people will find the cheapest way to move it.

caption: A bounty meant to wipe out rats ended with people breeding them. That's Goodhart's law: once a number becomes the target, it stops telling you the truth.
